\begin{abstract}
Residential electric-vehicle (EV) charging concentrates in the evening, when
energy is expensive and feeder voltages are lowest. Prices change hourly,
dispatch every few minutes and voltages within a minute, yet most learned
coordinators act at one rate. We propose a
nested controller with one level per timescale. Proximal policy optimization
sets an hourly price corridor. A shared deep deterministic policy
gradient agent dispatches every \SI{15}{min} as a learned residual on a
deadline-aware cheapest-slot plan, and least-laxity-first allocation keeps
dispatch within charger and transformer limits. A non-learned layer
corrects voltage every \SI{60}{s} with charger reactive power bounded by the
inverter rating. On IEEE 33- and 69-bus feeders with AC power flow, real
prices and household loads, a synthetic residential fleet and, for
generalization, recorded workplace sessions (\GEvalDays{} held-out days), the
controller costs \GSavingNestedUncSThree\% less than uncoordinated charging at
\GPenSThree\% penetration without voltage violations% claim: nested_zero_viol_nominal
\ and is the cheapest learned controller,% claim: nested_cheapest_learned_main
\ but \GGapNestedPaSThree\% more than a price-aware heuristic.% claim: pa_cheaper_than_nested_all_main
\ Ablations attribute the cost gains to the planning prior% claim: abl_abl_no_prior_seed_separated_S3
\ and the absence of violations to the voltage layer.% claim: ablation_violates_S3
\ Attached to any baseline, it removes all
violations up to \GPenSFive\% penetration whenever the base load alone respects
the floor.% claim: l3_zero_viol_rules_nominal
% claim: l3_zero_viol_learned_nominal
% claim: s4_l3_violations_only_base_load_days
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
Deep reinforcement learning, distribution networks, electric vehicle charging,
multi-timescale control, reactive power, residual policy learning,
transportation electrification, voltage regulation.
\end{IEEEkeywords}

\section{Introduction}
\IEEEPARstart{E}{lectric} vehicles are becoming one of the largest flexible
loads on distribution feeders, and when they charge decides both what drivers
pay and whether voltages stay within limits. This section motivates the
problem, states its challenges, reviews prior work and lists our contributions.

\subsection{Background and Motivation}
Transportation electrification is accelerating: global
electric-car sales exceeded 17 million in 2024 and are expected to pass 20
million in 2025~\cite{iea2025}. Residential charging of electric vehicles (EVs)
concentrates in the evening, when household demand peaks. On weak radial
feeders it depresses end-of-line voltages toward and below the $0.95\pu$ lower
limit of the ANSI C84.1 service range~\cite{ansi_c84,clement2010,stiasny2021}
and buys energy in the most expensive hours of the day-ahead market.
Coordination can avoid both, because most vehicles stay plugged in far longer
than they need to charge.

\subsection{Challenges}
\begin{enumerate}
\item \emph{Timescales:} prices change hourly, dispatch every few minutes and
voltages within seconds; one decision interval fits none of them well.
\item \emph{Run-time voltage safety:} learned coordinators that model voltage
treat its limits as reward penalties or expected costs, not enforced at run time.
\item \emph{Feasibility:} per-vehicle rates must respect charger, transformer
and deadline limits, which penalties teach only approximately.
\item \emph{Evidence:} learned controllers are rarely compared with strong
model-based references, with the same voltage correction for all, over many
held-out days and seeds.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Related Work and Research Gap}
Optimization-based schedulers~\cite{clement2010,ortegavazquez2014} need
vehicle-level forecasts over the whole horizon and, to see the network, a
network model.
Decentralized schemes such as time-of-use (TOU) tariffs, game-theoretic demand
response and priority rules~\cite{mohsenian2010,ma2013,xu2016priority} scale
well but do not observe the network; serving vehicles with less laxity
first~\cite{xu2016priority} underlies our allocation. Deep reinforcement
learning (RL) has scheduled real-time charging with deep Q-learning and price
features~\cite{wan2019} and with DDPG~\cite{zhang2020cddpg}, exploited the
structure of optimal policies in a distribution network~\cite{jin2020},
coordinated multiple agents and navigation~\cite{dasilva2020,park2022,qian2021},
added vehicle-to-grid operation and degradation~\cite{shibl2023}, controlled a
fleet~\cite{tuchnitz2021}, scaled with graph neural
networks~\cite{orfanoudakis2025} and priced charging
stations~\cite{zhao2022pricing}; EV2Gym~\cite{orfanoudakis2025ev2gym} and
SustainGym~\cite{yeh2023sustaingym} provide benchmarks and, here, the open
data. Hierarchical designs coordinate several stations~\cite{saner2022} or
regulate voltage on two timescales for flash-charged buses~\cite{wang2025flash};
hierarchical RL is surveyed in~\cite{pateria2021}. Safe RL handles constraints such as
voltage limits as expected costs (CPO~\cite{achiam2017} and Lagrangian methods,
reviewed in~\cite{su2025review}) and has been applied to Volt-VAR
control~\cite{wang2020voltvar}, active distribution
networks~\cite{kou2020}, stability-constrained~\cite{shi2022stability} and
multi-agent~\cite{wang2024safemarl} voltage control; multi-agent deep RL also
coordinates Volt-VAR devices~\cite{gao2021consensus} and active and reactive
power~\cite{hu2022voltage}. EV chargers have supported
voltage with vehicle-to-grid active power~\cite{singh2013,mattos2024}, reactive
power~\cite{leemput2015,hu2021dmpc} or both~\cite{wang2023coord}; inverter
reactive capability is standardized in IEEE Std 1547-2018~\cite{ieee1547}.

Table~\ref{tab:positioning} summarizes the gap. \emph{Nested
learning}~\cite{behrouz2025} views a learning system as interconnected
optimization problems, each updated at its own frequency; we use it as a design
principle, with one level per timescale and feasibility and voltage safety
kept out of the learning problem.

\subsection{Contributions}
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{A nested controller} (Section~\ref{sec:method}): an hourly
price-corridor policy trained with proximal policy optimization (PPO), a shared
15-min dispatch policy trained with deep deterministic policy gradient (DDPG)
and a non-learned 60-s voltage layer.
\item \textbf{Plan-residual dispatch, feasible by construction.} Level~2 learns
a correction to a deadline-aware cheapest-slot plan (residual policy
learning~\cite{silver2018residual,johannink2019residual}); least-laxity-first
(LLF) allocation with a deadline guard maps it to per-vehicle rates within
charger and transformer limits.
\item \textbf{Reactive correction bounded by the inverter rating.} Level~3 uses
$\Qmax_i=\sqrt{S_i^2-P_i^2}$~\cite{leemput2015}, so curtailment never removes
headroom; a secant step on the measured sensitivity closes the voltage gap,
with curtailment as fallback, for every baseline as well.
\item \textbf{A reproducible, paired evaluation} (Sections~\ref{sec:system}
and~\ref{sec:setup}): AC power flow on two IEEE feeders; ENTSO-E
prices~\cite{hirth2018}, Pecan Street loads~\cite{pecanstreet} and ACN-Data
sessions~\cite{lee2019acn}; \GEvalDays{} held-out days; \GTrainSeedsWord{}
training seeds; eight baselines, including model-predictive control (MPC) with
a linear-programming optimal power flow (LP-OPF) and perfect foresight,
PPO-Lagrangian, constrained policy optimization (CPO) and hierarchical RL
(HRL); one command regenerates every result.
\end{enumerate}

Sections~\ref{sec:system}--\ref{sec:setup} present the system, controller and
setup, Sections~\ref{sec:results} and~\ref{sec:discussion} the results and their
scope, and Section~\ref{sec:conclusion} concludes.

\section{System Model and Study Design}
\label{sec:system}
We first fix the setting in which the controller acts: feeders, data, the
drivers' price response and the metrics by which every method is judged.

\subsection{Feeder and Power Flow}
We use the IEEE 33-bus~\cite{baran1989} and 69-bus~\cite{baran1989cap} radial
feeders with the MATPOWER data~\cite{zimmerman2011} (open tie lines removed).
Five aggregators connect at electrically strong and weak buses
(Table~\ref{tab:setup}); vehicles are assigned to them
at random in proportions 0.18, 0.18, 0.19, 0.19 and 0.26, and aggregator $k$
serves them through a transformer of rating $P^{\mathrm{cap}}_k=\SI{500}{kW}$.
With constant-power loads the radial AC power-flow equations are
\begin{equation}
\mathbf{V}=V_0\mathbf{1}-\mathbf{Z}^{\mathrm{path}}\left(\mathbf{S}\oslash\mathbf{V}\right)^{*},
\label{eq:pf}
\end{equation}
where $\mathbf{V}$ and $\mathbf{S}$ hold the complex voltages and loads of the
non-substation buses, $V_0=1.03\pu$ is the substation voltage, $\mathbf{1}$ is
the all-ones vector, $\oslash$ is element-wise division, $(\cdot)^*$ is
element-wise conjugation and $Z^{\mathrm{path}}_{nm}$ is the impedance of the
path shared by buses $n$ and $m$ from the substation. We solve~\eqref{eq:pf}
every \SI{60}{s} by the backward/forward sweep~\cite{shirmohammadi1988} to
$10^{-10}\pu$; our tests match pandapower's Newton--Raphson
solution~\cite{thurner2018} to $10^{-8}\pu$.

\subsection{Data, Fleets and Driver Response}
Day-ahead prices from the ENTSO-E Transparency Platform~\cite{hirth2018} and
the 15-min consumption of 25 Pecan Street homes~\cite{pecanstreet}, both as
distributed with EV2Gym~\cite{orfanoudakis2025ev2gym}, drive the simulation
(Table~\ref{tab:setup}). The household profile, normalized by its 99.5th
percentile and matched by day of year (so training and test days share it),
scales the nominal feeder loads. The scale is the largest value (in steps of
0.01) for which the feeder \emph{without} EVs stays at or above $0.955\pu$
over the whole year, so the voltage problems studied here are caused by EV
charging. The main experiments use a synthetic residential fleet with the
stated distributions of Table~\ref{tab:setup} (initial state of charge clipped
to $[0.05,0.9]$, target at least 0.05 above it, battery classes equally likely)
and chargers of rating $\bar c=\SI{11}{kW}$ and efficiency $\eta=0.95$. For
generalization we use real sessions from ACN-Data~\cite{lee2019acn} at Caltech
and JPL (bundled with SustainGym~\cite{yeh2023sustaingym}): each sampled
vehicle keeps a recorded session's arrival, dwell and delivered energy (2019
for training, 2020--2021 for testing, weekdays, episodes from 06:00).
Requests are capped at what the charger can deliver during the dwell.

Price response is part of the environment, not a control level. Each vehicle
accepts the execution price $p_k$ of its aggregator with the Fishbein--Ajzen
attitude model~\cite{fishbein1975},
\begin{equation}
P^{\mathrm{acc}}_i=\sigma\!\left(w^{\mathrm{c}}_i\frac{\lambda^{\mathrm{ref}}-p_k}{\lambda^{\mathrm{ref}}}+w^{\mathrm{n}}_i\bar A+b_i\right),
\label{eq:fishbein}
\end{equation}
with logistic $\sigma$, reference rate $\lambda^{\mathrm{ref}}$, last-interval
fleet acceptance $\bar A$ (floored at 0.3) and the heterogeneous weights of
Table~\ref{tab:setup}. A driver whose remaining need exceeds 0.7 times the
charger rating times the hours to departure accepts regardless of price.
Acceptance is drawn once per dispatch interval.

\subsection{Energy Accounting and Metrics}
\label{sec:metrics}
A vehicle draws power only while plugged in, having accepted the price and
still needing energy. The energy cost is the day-ahead price times the energy
drawn after any curtailment. We report the daily cost (\euro), the cost per
delivered kWh, the service quality (SQ, delivered over requested energy), the
violation rate (Viol., share of 60-s steps with a bus below $\vlim=0.95\pu$
after any correction), the mean daily minimum voltage (lowest bus voltage
$V^{\min}$ of each day, averaged over days; $V^{\min}$ denotes the lowest bus
voltage of the period considered), curtailed (Curt.) and unmet energy (need
left at departure), both in kWh per day, and the mean retail price paid
(Retail). Fig.~\ref{fig:pipeline} summarizes the study from data to results.

\section{Nested Controller}
\label{sec:method}
The controller splits coordination by timescale, so that each decision is
taken at the rate at which its inputs change. Fig.~\ref{fig:arch} shows the
architecture: each level is a decision process at its own rate whose
environment includes the drivers' price response and the faster levels.

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{generated/fig_architecture.pdf}
\caption{Nested controller and simulated environment. Solid arrows are set
points and data passed down; dashed arrows are measurements fed back. Labels
name the quantity passed; numbers in parentheses refer to equations.}
\label{fig:arch}
\end{figure*}

\subsection{Level 1: Price Corridor (PPO, Hourly)}
The state $s^{(1)}_t\in\mathbb{R}^{11}$ holds the mean bus voltage, substation
$P$ and $Q$, current price, plugged-in share, mean state of charge,
line-loading margin (rating \SI{0.4}{kA}), substation loading (\SI{8}{MVA}),
the hour (sine, cosine) and the mean price over the next 12\,h. The action $a^{(1)}_t\in[0,1]^2$, drawn from Beta
distributions, sets the center $c_t$ and width $w_t$ of the corridor
$[p^{\min}_t,p^{\max}_t]=[c_t-w_t/2,\,c_t+w_t/2]$, clipped to
$[p^{\mathrm{lo}},p^{\mathrm{hi}}]=[\text{\euro}0.05,\text{\euro}0.40]/\mathrm{kWh}$:
\begin{align}
c_t&=\lambda^{\mathrm{ref}}+(2a^{(1)}_{t,1}-1)\begin{cases}\lambda^{\mathrm{ref}}-p^{\mathrm{lo}}, & a^{(1)}_{t,1}<0.5,\\ p^{\mathrm{hi}}-\lambda^{\mathrm{ref}}, & \text{otherwise,}\end{cases}\nonumber\\
w_t&=w^{\min}+a^{(1)}_{t,2}\,(w^{\max}-w^{\min}),
\end{align}
with $w^{\min}=\text{\euro}0.02$ and $w^{\max}=\text{\euro}0.20/\mathrm{kWh}$.
The neutral action $(0.5,0.5)$ gives the \emph{neutral corridor}
$[\text{\euro}\GNeutralLo,\text{\euro}\GNeutralHi]/\mathrm{kWh}$ around the
reference rate, so an untrained policy charges about the flat tariff of the
baselines. The reward of hour $t$,
\begin{align}
r^{(1)}_t={}&-\frac{C_t}{100}-50\,(20\,\Delta V_t)^2-10\,\mathbb{I}[\Delta V_t>0]\nonumber\\
&-5\,\frac{U_t}{100}-0.5\,\frac{X_t}{100}+\omega\,\frac{R_t-\lambda^{\mathrm{ref}}E^{\mathrm{del}}_t}{100},
\label{eq:r1}
\end{align}
penalizes energy cost $C_t$, the voltage deficit
$\Delta V_t=\max(0,\vlim-V^{\min}_t)$ ($\mathbb{I}$: indicator), unmet energy
$U_t$ of departing vehicles and curtailment $X_t$; the last term, with retail
revenue $R_t$ and delivered energy $E^{\mathrm{del}}_t$, enforces revenue
neutrality (below). PPO~\cite{schulman2017} trains the policy (clipping 0.2,
$\gamma=0.99$, generalized advantage estimation (GAE) with
$\lambda_{\mathrm{GAE}}=0.95$).

\subsection{Level 2: Plan-Residual Dispatch (DDPG, 15 min)}
\emph{State.} The state $s^{(2)}_{\tau,k}\in\mathbb{R}^{28}$ of aggregator $k$
holds its bus voltage, the hour, the prices of the current and next 11 hours,
the corridor, the number of plugged-in vehicles, their remaining need (total
and in four laxity bins: below 1, 1--3, 3--6 and above 6\,h), the power they
can absorb, their mean remaining dwell, the last acceptance rate and the plan
set point $u^0_{\tau,k}$. One actor $\mu$ and one critic are shared by the
five aggregators, with a one-hot identifier (parameter sharing~\cite{gupta2017}).

\emph{Planning prior.} For each plugged-in vehicle $i$ with remaining need
$e_i$, the plan selects the $\lceil e_i/(\eta\bar c\Delta)\rceil$ cheapest
intervals before departure ($\Delta=\SI{15}{min}$; prices beyond the 12-h
look-ahead are valued at their known mean). The plan set point
$u^0_{\tau,k}\in[0,1]$ is the power of the vehicles whose current interval is
selected, as a fraction of the power the aggregator can deliver now; it uses
only the price look-ahead and the needs and departures of plugged-in vehicles.

\emph{Action.} The actor output $a_{\tau,k}=\mu(s^{(2)}_{\tau,k})\in[0,1]^2$
corrects the plan and sets the execution price inside the corridor:
\begin{align}
u_{\tau,k}&=\mathrm{clip}\big(u^0_{\tau,k}+\rho\,(2a_{\tau,k,1}-1),\,0,\,1\big),
\label{eq:residual}\\
p_{\tau,k}&=p^{\min}_t+a_{\tau,k,2}\,(p^{\max}_t-p^{\min}_t),
\end{align}
so $a_{\tau,k,1}=0.5$ reproduces the plan (residual scale $\rho$ in
Table~\ref{tab:hyper}).

\emph{Feasibility by construction.} Let $\hat c_i=\min\{\bar c,\,e_i/(\eta\Delta)\}$
for the vehicles that accepted the price. The set point dispatches
$P_{\tau,k}=u_{\tau,k}\min\{P^{\mathrm{cap}}_k,\sum_i\hat c_i\}$, filled in
order of increasing laxity $\ell_i=h_i-e_i/(\eta\bar c)$ ($h_i$: hours to
departure)~\cite{xu2016priority}; a deadline guard raises $P_{\tau,k}$ to cover
every vehicle with $\ell_i\le\Delta$, up to the same limit. Every dispatch
therefore lies in
\begin{equation}
\mathcal{C}_k=\Big\{c:\ 0\le c_i\le\hat c_i,\ \textstyle\sum_i c_i\le P^{\mathrm{cap}}_k\Big\}.
\end{equation}
Per-vehicle rates of other methods are projected onto $\mathcal{C}_k$.

\emph{Reward.} The reward of aggregator $k$ in interval $\tau$ is
\begin{align}
r^{(2)}_{\tau,k}={}&-C_{\tau,k}+\omega\,(p_{\tau,k}-\lambda^{\mathrm{ref}})E^{\mathrm{del}}_{\tau,k}\nonumber\\
&-2\,U_{\tau,k}-0.5\,G_{\tau,k}-0.5\,X_{\tau,k},
\label{eq:r2}
\end{align}
with the interval's energy cost $C_{\tau,k}$ (summing to the daily cost), unmet
energy $U_{\tau,k}$ of departing vehicles, energy $G_{\tau,k}$ that can no
longer be delivered before departure and curtailed energy $X_{\tau,k}$ (kWh;
money in \euro). With 96 decisions per day we use $\gamma=0.999$; $\gamma=0.99$
would discount a cost 12\,h ahead by almost 40\%.

\emph{Revenue-neutral pricing.} A profit-seeking aggregator would raise prices,
lowering acceptance and pushing charging into expensive hours. We instead
require the mean retail price paid to equal the flat rate
$\lambda^{\mathrm{ref}}$ of the non-pricing baselines; $\omega$
in~\eqref{eq:r1} and~\eqref{eq:r2} is the multiplier of this constraint,
updated after every episode by a proportional--integral (PI)
rule~\cite{stooke2020pid} because plain dual ascent oscillated:
\begin{align}
\varepsilon&=(\lambda^{\mathrm{ref}}-\bar p)/\lambda^{\mathrm{ref}},\qquad \bar\varepsilon\leftarrow(1-\alpha)\,\bar\varepsilon+\alpha\,\varepsilon,\nonumber\\
\omega&=\mathrm{clip}\Big(K_p\,\bar\varepsilon+K_i\textstyle\sum\varepsilon,\ \omega^{\min},\ \omega^{\max}\Big),
\end{align}
where $\bar p$ is the episode's mean retail price paid, $\bar\varepsilon$ an
exponential moving average (EMA) with weight $\alpha$, and the sum over past
episodes is clipped against wind-up (Table~\ref{tab:hyper}). Since this holds
the constraint only on average over training, a constant price offset (the sum
clipped to $[p^{\mathrm{lo}},p^{\mathrm{hi}}]$) is then calibrated by bisection
on ten 2023 training days so that the deterministic policy's mean retail price
equals $\lambda^{\mathrm{ref}}$; this calibration is applied to every learned
method and moved prices by at most \euro\GCalibOffsetAbsmax/kWh.

DDPG~\cite{lillicrap2016} trains actor and critic (256--128--64 units) on the
action \emph{actually applied} after the guard, mapped back
through~\eqref{eq:residual} and clipped to $[0,1]$; the actor's output layer
starts near zero, so training starts from the plan.

\subsection{Level 3: Reactive Voltage Correction (60 s)}
Level~3 runs inside every 60-s step (Fig.~\ref{fig:l3}). If
$\min_n|V_n|<\vlim+\delta$ after the power flow ($\delta=0.001\pu$), the
plugged-in chargers at aggregator bus $k$ offer the headroom
\begin{equation}
\bar Q_k=\sum_{i\in k}\sqrt{\max\{S_i^2-P_i^2,\,0\}},\qquad S_i=\SI{12}{kVA},
\end{equation}
so a charger still offers \GQFullPower\,kvar at its full \GPCharger\,kW and its
full rating at $P_i=0$, and curtailing active power \emph{increases} the
headroom ($S_i$ bounds only the reactive capability; the 11-kW active-power
limit is separate). The first injection is proportional to the voltage gap,
saturates at $V^{\min}=0.90\pu$ and is weighted toward the most depressed
aggregator buses. Later iterations measure the sensitivity
$\hat s=\Delta V^{\min}/\Delta Q$ between the last two power flows and, if
$\Delta Q$ and $\Delta V^{\min}$ are both positive, take the secant step
\begin{equation}
\Delta Q=1.2\,\big(\vlim+\delta-V^{\min}\big)/\hat s,
\end{equation}
split by voltage depression and capped by the remaining headroom; otherwise
the proportional step is repeated. Without headroom, EV power is shed in steps
of up to 20\% per iteration, most at the most depressed bus. The loop stops
when $V^{\min}\ge\vlim+\delta$ or after eight corrective power flows (twenty
once curtailment has started). Measured on successive AC solutions, the step
needs no precomputed network model. Level~3 is independent of the policy above
it, so we also attach it to every baseline (``+L3'').

\caption{Level-3 correction inside one 60-s step.}
\label{fig:l3}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Training}
Episodes are random 2023 days. A curriculum raises the fleet from 60 to 300
vehicles in steps of 60 when the last 20 episodes reach mean SQ $\ge0.95$ with
mean curtailment $\le\SI{20}{kWh}$; the final stage draws 120 to 300 vehicles.
Each run has \GTrainEpisodes{} episodes (about \GTrainHoursNested~h on one CPU
core); Table~\ref{tab:hyper} lists the hyperparameters.

\section{Experimental Setup}
\label{sec:setup}
A fair test needs strong alternatives, stressed conditions and many
independent days; this section defines all three.

\subsection{Scenarios}
Table~\ref{tab:scendef} defines the scenarios. S1, S2, S3 and S5 vary the
penetration. S4 repeats S3 with an hourly-persistent deviation of the base load
from its profile (standard deviation 15\%, clipped to $\pm40\%$), a forecast
error for the LP-OPF, the only method that uses a load forecast. Two stress
tests probe Level~3: S6 forbids charging between 19:00 and 20:00, so that
charging resumes in a synchronized rebound, and S7 emulates reduced reactive
capability by halving the inverter rating to $S_i=\GSRatedSSeven$\,kVA, so a
charger drawing more than \SI{6}{kW} offers no reactive power.

\subsection{Baselines}
\emph{Rule-based:} uncoordinated charging (full power on arrival); a TOU timer
(off-peak 23:00--07:00, earlier only when laxity is exhausted; tariff
\text{\euro}0.12/kWh off-peak, \text{\euro}0.30/kWh 17:00--21:00 and
\text{\euro}0.20/kWh otherwise); and the price-aware heuristic, i.e., the
Level-2 plan executed per vehicle at full power with the same 12-h look-ahead.
\emph{Model-predictive LP-OPF$^\ast$:} at every interval an LP over the rest of
the day (HiGHS~\cite{huangfu2018}) minimizes energy cost plus
\text{\euro}5/kWh of unmet energy subject to energy, charger and transformer
limits and linearized voltage limits ($\ge\vlim+\delta$) from
finite-difference sensitivities at the forecast no-EV operating point. The
asterisk marks \emph{perfect foresight} of prices and of every vehicle's
arrival, departure and need. It is a strong reference, neither deployable nor a
strict bound: its voltage model is linearized and drivers may decline.
\emph{Learned:} flat DDPG (one agent for all aggregators), PPO-Lagrangian and
CPO~\cite{achiam2017} (expected-cost constraint on violations, limit $d=0$) and
a goal-conditioned HRL agent (hourly DDPG goals, 15-min DDPG workers). They
observe the same states, use the same allocation, reward terms, discount and
revenue-neutral multiplier, and price inside the neutral corridor; flat DDPG
and HRL add a voltage penalty (HRL workers also a goal-tracking term). All are
evaluated with and without Level~3. The non-pricing baselines charge
$\lambda^{\mathrm{ref}}$.

\subsection{Protocol}
All methods are evaluated on the same \GEvalDays{} distinct 2024 days with
identical fleets and noise (paired design); learned methods use
\GTrainSeedsWord{} training seeds (\GAuxSeedsWord{} in ablations and
generalization), averaged per day. We report means with 95\% bootstrap
confidence intervals over days (10\,000 resamples) and Holm-corrected Wilcoxon
signed-rank tests on the paired daily differences. The allocation rule was
fixed before testing on \GTuneValDays{} held-out 2023 days by a pre-specified
criterion: over three variants that serve planned slots first
(\GTuneSeedsWord{} seeds each), the S3 cost fell by up to
\GTuneCostReductionMax\%,% claim: tune_plan_cheaper_S3
\ but \GTuneUnmetIncreaseMinSThree\%--\GTuneUnmetIncreaseMaxSThree\% (S3) and
\GTuneUnmetIncreaseMinSSeven\%--\GTuneUnmetIncreaseMaxSSeven\% (S7) more energy
was left undelivered,% claim: tune_plan_more_unmet
\ so least-laxity-first allocation was kept.% claim: tune_llf_selected
